**June 23, 1956 — a Saturday**

The America you entered was Eisenhower's America — prosperous, suburban, and increasingly uneasy beneath the surface. The Korean War was three years over. The economy was growing. New highways were reaching toward new subdivisions. But beneath the confidence ran a Cold War current that no amount of prosperity could fully suppress: the Soviet Union had tested a hydrogen bomb in 1953, and both superpowers were conducting atmospheric nuclear tests that were depositing radioactive fallout in the world's food and water. Civil defense drills taught schoolchildren to duck and cover. The gap between the advertised version of American life and its actual tensions was at its widest.

---

**Egypt's president — on the exact day you were born**

On June 23, 1956, Gamal Abdel Nasser was confirmed as Egypt's first President under a new constitution, winning a referendum with overwhelming — if uncontested — support. For Nasser and for Egypt, the moment carried weight beyond a formal title: it represented the consolidation of a postcolonial national identity, a deliberate break from decades of British occupation. Nasser was 38 years old, charismatic, and watching carefully what the Western powers would do next. They would give him his answer within the month.

---

**Six days later: the Interstate Highway System**

On June 29, 1956 — six days after your birth — President Eisenhower signed the Federal Aid Highway Act, authorizing the construction of 41,000 miles of interstate highway across the United States. It was the largest public works project in American history, justified publicly as a civil defense measure but transformative in ways that had nothing to do with defense. The interstate system reshaped American geography, accelerated suburbanization, gutted urban rail networks, and created the physical infrastructure of American life for the next half-century. The country you grew up in was built, in significant part, on roads authorized six days after you arrived.

---

**±30 days: The decision that started the Suez Crisis**

Twenty-six days after your birth, on July 19, 1956, Secretary of State John Foster Dulles abruptly withdrew the American offer to fund Egypt's Aswan High Dam — citing Egypt's dealings with the Soviet bloc, and doing so in terms that were deliberately humiliating. Nasser's response came one week later: on July 26, he nationalized the Suez Canal Company, announcing Egypt would use canal revenues to build the dam itself.

What followed was one of the defining crises of the postwar order. Britain, France, and Israel coordinated a military attack on Egypt in late October 1956. Eisenhower, furious at being deceived by allies, forced all three to withdraw under American pressure — ending British and French pretensions to independent imperial power and establishing, beyond any remaining doubt, that the United States and Soviet Union were the only forces that truly mattered in the new world order. The Suez Crisis is considered the moment when the age of European empires definitively closed. It was set in motion by a decision made 26 days after you were born, involving a man who had been elected president the day you were born.

---

**The year also produced Hungary**

1956 did not spend its upheaval on Suez alone. In October, as the Suez Crisis unfolded, Hungarian citizens rose against Soviet-backed communist rule — students, workers, and soldiers in the streets of Budapest, Soviet tanks responding with force. The Hungarian Revolution was crushed within days. Thousands were killed; 200,000 fled. The world watched and the West did nothing enforceable. It was the most dramatic Cold War confrontation between 1953 and 1989 — and it happened while you were four months old, in the same year your life began.

---

**The arc of 70 years**

You turned 70 this past June. You were born the year the Suez Crisis began, the year Hungary rose and was crushed, the year the American interstate system was authorized, the year a postcolonial leader reshaped the map of global power.

In 70 years: legal segregation ended. Vietnam began and ended. Humans walked on the Moon. The Berlin Wall rose and fell. The Soviet Union dissolved. Apartheid ended. The personal computer arrived. The internet connected the world.

You entered a world where radio and the daily newspaper were the primary media, where computing was institutional, where the fastest communication between continents required days. You inhabit 2026, where those constraints have dissolved so completely that describing them requires effort. The distance between those two worlds is your life — and you have watched every mile of it close.
